To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two novel prostate-specific androgen-regulated ETV4 fusion partner genes have been identified in prostate cancer: CANT1 and KLK2.
we have identified two new ETV4 gene fusion partners in prostate cancer, KLK2 and CANT1, and that both genes are androgen-induced and have a prostate-specific expression pattern.
we identified two novel prostate-specific androgen-regulated ETV4 fusion partner genes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel prostate-specific androgen-regulated ETV4 fusion transcripts in prostate cancer.
the discovery and functional characterization of the first two novel prostate-specific androgen-regulated ETV4 fusion partner genes in prostate cancer.
the identification of novel androgen-regulated and prostate-specific fusion genes in prostate cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TMPRSS2-ERG and the two newly described KLK2- and CANT1 fusions are the most common prostate cancer-specific fusion genes.
ETV4 is a novel fusion partner of KLK2 and CANT1, and that these fusion genes are androgen regulated and prostate specific.
the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion gene is the most common fusion in prostate cancer, but TMPRSS2 is only the most frequent partner gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the TMPRSS2-ERG, TMPRSS2ETV1 and now TMPRSS2- ETV4 fusion events are the most frequent ETS family gene fusions in prostate cancer and that the KLK2- ETV1, KLK2-ETS and CANT1ETV4 fusion events are additional examples for prostate-specific androgen-regulated ETS family gene fusion partners in prostate cancer.
TMPRSS2-ERG and KLK2- and CANT1-fusions with ETV4, all three of which have been shown to be prostate-specific androgen-induced, are the most frequent genetic alterations in prostate cancer.
the two novel ETS gene fusions in prostate cancer have a unique combination of prostate-specificity and androgen-regulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion is only the tip of the iceberg.
ETV4 can be fused to prostate-specific genes, and that the ETV4 fusion partner can be an androgen-regulated gene.
ETV4 is the second most frequent prostate-specific and androgendriven fusion partner of the TMPRSS2 gene.
